title: Stoic in failure
hookLine: return, and be glad of what went well

lines: MARCUS NEEDED A RULE FOR FAILING.
cards: Day twelve of the new habit. Eleven days of getting up early, and this morning you hit snooze three times and lay there scrolling.

Or it's bigger: the job interview that went badly, the diet that collapsed at a birthday party, the promise to yourself about drinking, broken again. And the voice arrives: see, you always do this. Might as well quit.
The emperor of Rome wrote about this in his private notebook. He fell short of his own rules often enough to need a rule for falling short.

teach.b: First, the rule. In book five of the Meditations, Marcus tells himself: don't be disgusted, discouraged or dissatisfied if you don't manage to do everything by right principles.

teach.h: RETURN, AS TO A SOOTHING REMEDY.
teach.b: When you've been knocked off course, return. And be content if the greater part of what you do is worthy of a human being.
Three moves: no disgust, return, be glad of the greater part. Second, how to return.
Don't go back to philosophy as to a schoolmaster with a cane, Marcus adds, but the way someone with sore eyes goes back to the soothing sponge.
Not starting over from zero: returning to the practice, as if it had been waiting for you. A missed day is not a broken streak of character. It's a step off the path, and the path is still there.
Third, being glad of what went well. This is the part people skip. Love the practice you return to, Marcus says, and be content with the larger share done well.
Eleven early mornings aren't erased by one late one. They happened. They count.
He compares the student to an athlete: a fall in the contest doesn't stop you from contending again.

If you slip, he tells his students, don't give up on yourself; begin again. Put Marcus and Epictetus together, and the Stoic in failure isn't someone who never fails. It's someone who's very good at coming back.

how: Some Stoic practitioners meet failure by returning to their practice without self-disgust and counting what went well, following Marcus Aurelius's advice in Meditations 5.9.

o: Epictetus's lectures, written down by his student
Seneca's letters to a friend about starting over
Marcus's notebook: no disgust at slipping; simply return

p: be content if it was worthy
not erased by one late one

s: Marcus says one failure cancels all your previous effort
be content if the greater part of what you do is worthy of a human being.
Marcus told himself not to be disgusted when he failed at his principles
Meditations 5.9: not disgusted, discouraged or dissatisfied.
Epictetus compared students to athletes who fall in training
what matters is getting up and beginning again.

games.q: you broke a habit you'd kept for eleven days. you're Marcus. what do you tell yourself?
o: return, and be glad of the greater part
start over from zero with a stricter plan
games.why: Meditations 5.9: don't be discouraged; return, and be content if most of what you do is worthy.

practice: Think of one recent failure, a habit dropped, a promise broken, a day that went wrong, and hear the voice that says you always do this, without arguing.
Then count, honestly, what went well before it: the days, the efforts, the times you kept going. Picture yourself stepping back onto the path, not from zero, and notice the very next small step.

wordCard.voice: Meditations, Marcus's book where he tells himself: no disgust at falling short, simply return, and be glad of the greater part done well. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: return. The path is still there, and so are the good days behind you. Day six hundred eighty-three counts.
